item.title: It's Time to Stop Using Ultrasonic Bark Deterrents
item.description:
Animal Behavior

It's Time to Stop Using Ultrasonic Bark Deterrents

These devices pose psychological risks, have unproven safety and rarely work.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Major veterinary behavior groups recommends against using ultrasonic bark deterrents.
  • When ultrasonic bark deterrents are used, faulty microphones punish dogs for barks they didn't make.
  • Risks of ultrasonic bark deterrents include chronic hyperarousal and harms to dog's hearing.

I get a steady stream of emails from people whose dogs have become anxious, reactive, or simply different since an ultrasonic bark deterrent entered the house. I wrote about these devices years ago. I've since spent a lot more time with the research, the manufacturers, and the product manuals—including as a consultant on a legal case—and I want to say something plainly that I only implied before:

We should stop using these devices on our own dogs.

Understanding Ultrasonic Bark Deterrents

Ultrasonic bark deterrents—fences, collars, and freestanding units—emit a sharp pulse of sound, usually around 24–25 kHz at 110–120 decibels, pitched above human hearing but well within a dog's range. A microphone detects barking and triggers the pulse. The theory is simple: Make barking unpleasant enough, often enough, and the dog stops.

No one can tell you these devices are safe. I called the companies that make them. Every representative told me their product was safe, but not one could produce a study. One rep at a bark-deterrent company thought safety testing might have been done back in 2003, possibly by "ASPA"—she meant the ASPCA, which has in fact publicly opposed these devices. Another told me the products must be safe because they're "sold everywhere, on Amazon and Chewy." That's not evidence. That's an absence of evidence being mistaken for its opposite—and it matters here because pet products face essentially no regulatory requirement to demonstrate safety or efficacy before they're sold to you.

In the absence of data, the precautionary principle applies: Assume potential for harm until shown otherwise. There are two harms worth separating.

They Operate at an Unsafe Decibel Range

Sound above roughly 80 decibels can damage a dog's ear; these devices run at 110–120.

High-frequency sound does attenuate quickly with distance, so a dog well away from the unit is probably safer than one close to it—but "probably" is doing real work in that sentence, because no one has actually studied what a 25 kHz pulse at that intensity does to a dog's hearing or nervous system over repeated exposure. Manufacturers' own manuals warn against use on puppies under a year and on dogs with existing hearing loss, which tells you the companies themselves suspect these devices aren't harmless—they just haven't funded the studies that would confirm it either way.

Sustained Hyperarousal Causes Psychological Harm

Among the potential harms, I think it's the more serious one. A dog exposed repeatedly to an unpredictable aversive sound experiences chronic activation of the stress response—cortisol, adrenaline, a nervous system primed for threat. Sustained hyperarousal is linked to anxiety, phobia development, inhibited learning, and increased reactivity and aggression.

Because the microphones are unsophisticated, they routinely misfire on wind, traffic, other dogs, even human voices—so a dog gets "corrected" for things she didn't do, with no way to learn what behavior the punishment was even for. That's not a training tool. It's a landscape of fear: a world that has started delivering unpredictable pain for reasons the dog can never work out. One company rep described the sound to me as being like fingernails on a chalkboard for a dog—offered as a casual reassurance, as though that were a small thing to inflict on a creature multiple times a day without warning.

Ultrasonic Bark Deterrents Are a Form of Punishment

Even setting the welfare question aside, these devices mostly don't work. Positive punishment gives an animal no information about what to do instead—only that something bad happens after barking, sometimes, unpredictably. Every major veterinary behavior organization that has taken a position on this agrees: The American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior warns that punishment-based approaches carry a documented risk of increased fear and aggression, and the Australian Veterinary Association is more blunt still, stating that punishment has no place in dog training.

Instead, Find the Reason for Your Dog's Barking

Barking is a real behavior with real causes—territorial alarm, fear, boredom, greeting, play—and treating all of them identically with an indiscriminate jolt of noise doesn't address any of them. Dogs habituate, they get more agitated, or they simply learn that their environment is untrustworthy. None of that is what anyone actually wants for their dog.

So: unproven safety, plausible and multiple pathways to harm, and a device that generally fails at the one job it's sold to do. That's not a marginal case against ultrasonic bark deterrents. That's a case for taking them off the shelf of things a loving dog owner reaches for.

If your dog barks more than you'd like, the fix is slower and less satisfying than a $50 box, but it actually works: Figure out why she's barking, then use positive reinforcement to teach an alternative. That's not a consolation prize. It's the only approach that gives your dog something to do besides be afraid.

item.title: The Vital Need for Hope
item.description:
Suicide

The Vital Need for Hope

Our well-being and will to live depend on keeping a sense of hope alive.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • The restoration of hope is an essential aspect of escaping despair and suicidal thinking.
  • Hope is more than a fleeting feeling—it is an attitude and cognitive skill set one can develop.
  • Sometimes, restoring one's sense of hope requires help from others.

September is Suicide Awareness Month, a time that carries profound personal gravity for me. I am intimately aware of the devastation and heartbreak of losing someone you love to suicide. My son, Wiley, died by suicide after a nine-year battle with bipolar II disorder. On one tragic day in September, his tenuous relationship with hope was overpowered by a suicidal state of mind. My heart goes out to anyone struggling with this kind of despair and hopelessness, and to those who have lost a loved one to suicide.

We can’t escape the reality that life can be incredibly difficult at times. A depressive episode or personal crisis can move in and temporarily hijack your ability to experience life’s goodness. It can make some people question whether life is worth living. In those moments, you need enough hope to compete with suicidal thoughts that try to convince you that the only solution for ending your suffering is to stop living. You need enough hope to believe there are other ways to address the sources of your pain, even if you haven’t found them yet. Hope reminds you that your life matters—that you matter.

Because our well-being and our will to live are dependent on maintaining this sense of hope, finding ways to keep it alive is vital. Research shows that hope is one of the strongest predictors of well-being and recovery from adversity. So let’s explore how to revitalize our sense of hope.

What Is Hope?

Hope should not be confused with simplistic positivity. It is much more grounded than that. Hope is not a passive belief or expectation that everything will be fine, nor is it a denial of real pain and difficulties. Hope does not demand that you act upbeat despite your circumstances.

Philosopher Albert Camus—who struggled with his own deep melancholy—described hope as an act of courage: the will to continue on, even when things feel bleak. Camus famously said, “In the midst of winter, I found there was within me an invincible summer.”

Psychologist C.R. Snyder views hope not as a fleeting emotion, but as a cognitive skill set we can develop. He provides a method for converting courage into action. Hope is built on three interconnected components: setting goals, mapping out pathways to reach them, and cultivating agency—the belief in your ability to make progress, however slowly, while flexibly dealing with obstacles along the way.

Hope lies somewhere between despair and blind optimism. Instead of asking, "Why bother?" it asks, "What next steps might help?" It accepts that while we cannot guarantee an outcome, we can try to influence our situation in a favorable direction. Hope is a perspective—a belief that things can improve, fueled by the willingness to keep pointing ourselves toward whatever light is shining through the cracks.

Cultivating Hope

Hope is more of a mindset that includes intentional actions, rather than a passive stance of simply waiting for a feeling or blessing to arrive. Here are a few ways to reawaken and nurture hope:

  • Get help addressing the sources of your suffering. When you are carrying the weight of real hardship and emotional suffering, it can be very hard to hold onto a sense of hope. Find people to turn to for support and let others help you understand and address what is troubling you and eroding your sense of hope.
  • Borrow hope from others. We often need to hold hope from others when our own feels depleted. If your sense of hope is waning, borrow hope from someone who is in a better state of mind, who can see the bigger picture and more possibilities than you currently can. You don’t need false reassurance—you need their empathy and a gentle reminder that things can change. They can be a source of hope for you until you are able to restore your own sense of hope.
  • Practice intentionality. Hope is an attitude and directional guide. Even when your thoughts and feelings are heavy, you can stay committed to taking "wise actions"—making decisions that align with your values, what really matters, and help you cope and recover. There is evidence that focusing on small, value-driven steps helps improve our lives and well-being. Desired results are not always immediately forthcoming, but remember that incremental, positive steps can make a cumulative, significant difference.
  • Find purpose. Connecting with our sense of purpose gives us a reason to live, reminding us that we have something to contribute. We often mistakenly think it must be something grand. Yet we can make a meaningful difference in quieter ways—being kind to others, offering a helping hand, taking care of your family or a pet, or solving a problem. If you’re in a difficult chapter and are struggling to connect to the unique gifts you have to offer, know they are still deep within. You can find your way back to the qualities you possess that positively impact others.
  • Savor good moments. Research shows that being on the lookout for, and creating more positive moments—such as feeling love, joy, interest, inspiration, and gratitude whenever you can—helps counter downward spirals. Noticing and keeping your mind and heart open to these types of experiences reminds us that goodness is possible.

May we all revitalize our sense of hope with attitudes and actions that demonstrate our willingness to courageously, patiently, and compassionately deal with our pain and suffering. May we keep our sense of hope alive—trust that things can get better and reach out for support when the weight of what we carry is too heavy to bear alone.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Couples Build Chemistry Through Shared Enjoyment
item.description:
Relationships

Couples Build Chemistry Through Shared Enjoyment

New research shows how savoring good moments may strengthen relationships.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • Savoring is a process involving focusing attention on experienced pleasure.
  • Joint savoring is mutual sharing of positive experiences between romantic partners.
  • Savoring experiences jointly is linked with quality of life and relationship well-being.
Source: Image by Alice Bitencourt from Pixabay

We all know couples who genuinely love to be together. They inspire us when they are newlyweds and encourage us when they celebrate their golden anniversary after 50 years of marital bliss.

But what is the secret? And for couples who don’t feel like role models for chemistry and contentment, how can they improve their relationship? The answer may be more straightforward than we think.

For Couples, Pleasurable Activities Are Better Together

Within relationships, as time goes by, some couples continue to bond, enjoying a deeper sense of love and intimacy as they get to know each other even better, while others grow apart. Alienation doesn’t happen overnight; it progresses over time as partners spend less time together, pursuing separate lives.

The good news is that by spending more quality time together, pursuing mutually enjoyable activities, partners can romantically reconnect and even take their relationship to an entirely new level. Research explains.

The Satisfaction of Joint Savoring

Noah B. Larsen et al. (2026) explored the concept of joint savoring in romantic relationships, investigating its effects as an interpersonal process. They define savoring as a process of focusing attention on sources of experienced pleasure, noting that it is linked with individual well-being in terms of mood, health, and decreased stress. They also found that it protects relationship satisfaction from perceptions and sources of stress. Regarding romantic relationships specifically, Larsen et al. note that general savoring enhances romantic relationship well-being in terms of communication and relationship satisfaction.

In their research, Larsen et al. investigated the potential benefits of joint savoring as a mutual process of sharing positive relational experiences between romantic partners. Using a nationwide sample of 589 individuals representing 589 couples, they found joint savoring was positively linked with quality of life and relationship well-being.

Among other findings, Larsen et al. found that individual reports of higher levels of joint savoring generally were linked to higher levels of romantic relationship well-being in terms of relationship confidence and couple satisfaction, and less communication conflict. They note this provides empirical support for the benefits of joint savoring for romantic relationship quality that are similar but distinct from the effects of general savoring. They explain that building upon the relational benefits of focusing on positive experiences external to the relationship, their findings highlight the advantages of positive experiences within the relationship.

Regarding stress, Larsen et al. noted that although previous research found a protective effect of general savoring for couple satisfaction in connection with a stressful life event, they did not find joint savoring in romantic relationships to have a protective effect upon couple satisfaction within a context of perceived stress. They suggest that apart from relationship confidence, the benefits of joint savoring between romantic partners may promote relationship outcomes directly, rather than through mitigating the effects of stress—real or perceived.

Romantic Relationship Maintenance

Larsen et al. acknowledge that their results add to other relationship maintenance strategies that couples use to protect and enhance the quality of their union, such as perceived gratitude, partner support, joint goals, and conflict management. And because joint savoring is linked with higher confidence in the relationship as well as better communication, there is great potential for relational improvement. And from sports to the symphony, adventure to the arts, there is no downside to sharing pleasurable activities with your partner, only an opportunity to renew romance.

item.title: How to Make Your September "Fresh Start" Last
item.description:
Self-Control

How to Make Your September "Fresh Start" Last

Change begins by listening to the parts of you with competing needs.

Posted September 19, 2026

Key points
  • September's "fresh start effect" encourages setting new goals and routines.
  • Usually, optimistic motivation doesn’t last because of conflict among the parts of a person's psyche.
  • Being willing to listen to the different voices inside may help with decision-making and commitment.

In 2014, researchers at Wharton pulled attendance records for 11,912 gym members tracked over 442 days. What they were looking for were points in time in which people’s attendance at the gym rose.

The researchers found that attendance wasn’t random. People came more at the start of new weeks, new months, and new academic semesters, and, of course, around New Year's Day.

This phenomenon was given a name: The "fresh start effect." The idea is that temporal landmarks create enough psychological distance from a "past self" that goals which originally felt stalled suddenly feel reachable.

A current landmark we’ve all just experienced is September. It’s relevant not just for people who started a new school year. For most of us, the transition from summer mode to our regular routine comes with the thought: Time to get back on track.

For some people, that means going back to the gym. For others, it’s finding the right meal prep routine, deciding to drink less, or just making a vague promise that this year, they'll eat better. This mindset of a fresh start probably sounds familiar to you, too. And if it is, maybe the next step is also familiar.

For many people, almost automatically, the desire that says, "I want to take care of myself" turns very quickly into, "I need to fix myself."

When a Fresh Start Becomes a Referendum

This new voice inside your head is not a completely different person; it’s more like a different part of you. Compared to the compassionate, positive first voice, the second voice is less confident in your abilities and is more critical.

You say to yourself, "I want more structure around food," then immediately feel exhausted from thinking about meal prep and counting calories. You want to use the new tracking app, but you simultaneously hate the idea of constantly monitoring yourself. Your first emotions are hope and happiness, but you also fear the moment this "new you" idea will fall apart, like it did in the past.

article continues after advertisement

None of that means you don't know what you want; it’s just that different parts of you may want different, and sometimes competing, things.

Why the Mind Doesn't Speak With One Voice

Internal family systems (IFS) is a therapeutic model based on the idea that our psyche contains different parts, each with its own perspective and protective function. Just like in a real "family," where one person is trying to set the rules while another is trying to break them—and yet another is trying to make everything feel better immediately—these different parts exist in each of us.

The IFS model of parts (the evidence for the clinical model is still developing—a 2025 scoping review found promising results but called for more rigorous research) reframes the idea that there should be one leading voice we should listen to when making resolutions about our habits, and in general. Instead of looking for one "winning voice," we can ask what each voice is trying to protect us from.

The Research on Eating Backs This Up

It might not be easy to give room to several voices inside us. It’s easier to think that there is one voice we should follow—the "smart voice" that knows what we should and shouldn't do. But often in real life, it can be difficult to make the decision we think we're supposed to make.

A 2025 Annual Review of Psychology paper analyzed years of research on self-control and eating and found a complicated system that affects our decision-making process: an interaction between reward sensitivity, emotion, habit, situational cues, and deliberate regulation often happens at the same time, as the relative weight of each varies by person and context.

article continues after advertisement

We judge it quickly as a lack of discipline, but on the inside, many competing processes are running at once. While you might hear a loud and clear voice that says, "I just need to be more disciplined," other voices pull you in different directions.

A Fresh Start Doesn't Have to Mean Starting Over

None of this means you shouldn't use September as a reset point. It’s actually a great opportunity to set new routines and name something you want to change.

Just try to remember that a new beginning doesn't have to become an indictment of who you were before. The part of you who is looking for more structure doesn’t have to defeat the part that wants more freedom; they can coexist and find balance. The desire to change doesn’t have to ignore the part of you that is already tired. The part that wants constant pleasure doesn’t have to run the show, but it can get some time to have fun.

This September, instead of asking yourself, "How do I finally become the person I want to be?" try asking, "Can I allow myself to listen to the different parts in me, without fear—and make a decision while leaving room for each of them?"
